content:
President Donald Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act into law on Wednesday, ordering the Justice Department to make public its files on the late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein within 30 days.

"I HAVE JUST SIGNED THE BILL TO RELEASE THE EPSTEIN FILES!" Trump wrote in a lengthy message on his Truth Social platform, according to Fox News. The signing came a day after Congress passed the measure with near-unanimous support: the House voted 427-1 on Tuesday, and the Senate approved it hours later by unanimous consent, skipping a formal roll call.

The law requires the Justice Department to publish all of its unclassified records, documents, communications and investigative materials related to the investigation and prosecution of Epstein in a searchable, downloadable format online. The material covers Epstein's sex trafficking case, his longtime associate Ghislaine Maxwell, who is serving a 20-year prison sentence, the internal communications of the department around the case, and the investigation into Epstein's death in a federal prison cell in August 2019. The 30-day deadline falls on December 19.

The department may withhold only limited categories of material, such as personally identifiable information of victims and material that could jeopardise an active federal investigation. The law expressly bars the department from withholding files to spare anyone embarrassment. Attorney General Pam Bondi told reporters on Wednesday that she would comply with the law, according to Fox News.

The signing closes a remarkable reversal. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump promised that, if elected, he would release documents related to the Epstein case. On July 7, however, the Justice Department and the Federal Bureau of Investigation issued a memorandum stating that there was no "incriminating client list", no evidence that Epstein's death was a murder, and that no further Epstein-related documents would be released, according to Xinhua. That memo set off months of pressure from lawmakers in both parties and from Epstein's survivors.

The bill itself was introduced in the House in mid-July, but Republican leaders, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, delayed the process for months. It reached the floor only because of a discharge petition led by Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, and Representative Ro Khanna, a California Democrat, which forced a vote once it gathered 218 signatures. The petition secured its final signature last Wednesday, Xinhua reported.

Two days before the House vote, Trump suddenly reversed his previous stance and called on Republican House members to vote in favour of releasing the files. US media suggested the turnaround was prompted by the fact that a substantial number of Republican representatives were already planning to vote for the measure. Trump had previously called the push a "Democrat hoax", but after signing the bill he said he had "nothing to hide".

The only lawmaker in Congress to oppose the bill was Representative Clay Higgins, a Louisiana Republican and a fervent supporter of Trump, who cast the lone "nay" vote in the House's 427-1 tally.

The final days before the vote were marked by a partisan fight over the files themselves. Democrats on the House Oversight Committee released Epstein-related documents involving Trump, and Republicans on the committee then released a far larger tranche of files as a countermeasure, accusing the Democrats of cherry-picking. On Friday, Trump directed the Justice Department to investigate high-profile Democrats connected to Epstein, including former President Bill Clinton. Critics viewed the move as an attempt to counter the impact of the documents involving Trump, according to Xinhua.

Attention now turns to what the department actually publishes — and what it blacks out. Survivors and lawmakers have said they will be watching the redactions closely. The law's supporters in Congress have warned that a heavily redacted release would defeat its purpose, and Massie and Khanna have said they intend to scrutinise the department's compliance once the deadline arrives.

The questions around Epstein's death are also likely to return to public view. The official finding is that Epstein died by suicide in his cell at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York on August 10, 2019, while awaiting trial on federal sex trafficking charges. That conclusion has been challenged, including by a forensic expert who recently argued the autopsy evidence points to homicide, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/forensic-expert-says-epstein-death-was-homicide-november-2026). The new law requires the department to release its files on the death investigation as well, which could settle — or deepen — the dispute.

For Trump, the signing ends a political problem that had dogged his administration for months, but it opens a new one: the files, once public, will be examined line by line by the press, by Congress and by the survivors who fought for them. The president has insisted the material will clear him. In 30 days, the public will be able to judge that claim for itself — and, as the [BBC reported](https://myrepublica.nagariknetwork.com/news/trump-signs-bill-ordering-to-release-epstein-files-49-26.html), the countdown has already begun.

The episode also fits a wider pattern of Trump's second term, in which court cases and legal fights involving the president have repeatedly become national political flashpoints, as [Global Wire reported in its coverage of his appeals](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-hush-money-appeals-november-2026). This time, however, the fight ended not in a courtroom but in a rare moment of bipartisan agreement: 427 members of the House and every senator present voted to force the files into the open.
summary: President Donald Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act into law on Wednesday, ending months of resistance and starting a 30-day countdown for the Justice Department to publish its unclassified Epstein records online after Congress passed the bill almost unanimously.
title: Trump signs Epstein Files Transparency Act, giving Justice Department 30 days to release the files
